Product Metrics for AI Features

Vaani Support Cloud · Bengaluru · September 2026

On the second Monday of September, Tara Raman, senior product manager at Vaani Support Cloud, opened a board slide titled "Copilot: Scale to 100%" and felt the same unease as three times before that quarter. Vaani sold helpdesk software to about ninety mid-sized Indian direct-to-consumer brands — apparel, skincare, small appliances — and eight months earlier her team had shipped Vaani Copilot, a feature that drafted a reply for a human agent every time a customer wrote in. The agent could send the draft as written, edit it, or discard it and start over. The pilot ran on one vertical, apparel returns and exchanges, covering roughly thirty-five percent of ticket volume across Vaani's customer base. The board had seen one number: drafting cost per ticket had fallen from about thirty rupees to under thirteen. Sundar Bhatt, the CFO, wanted Copilot on every ticket, every vertical, within sixty days. Rhea Fernandes, who ran trust and safety, had asked for two more weeks. Tara had four days to recommend one or the other, and the honest answer was that the cost number, taken alone, was answering the wrong question.

The idea

A product metric, in the ordinary sense, is a single number a team tracks to know whether something is working: signups, retention, revenue per user. An AI feature breaks that habit, because no single number can carry the weight. A large language model can produce an answer that is fluent, confidently wrong, expensive to generate, and unsafe to send, all at once — and a metric built for ordinary software, like "did the user complete the flow," misses every one of those failure modes except the first. The practice that emerged among product teams building AI copilots between roughly 2022 and 2024 — inside companies like GitHub, OpenAI and Anthropic, and taught at digital-product programmes at Wharton, Haas and Darden as an extension of the older discipline of North Star metric trees — is to insist on four numbers together, never one alone: task success (did the AI get the job done), acceptance and edit rate (how much a human had to change before trusting the output), cost per task (the full cost of one unit of AI-assisted work, not just the API bill), and safety (how often the output was wrong in a way that could hurt someone). None of the four is new by itself; what is new is the discipline of refusing to look at any one without the other three.

"An AI feature is not one metric but four working together — whether it gets the job done, whether people trust it enough to use as-is, what each use actually costs, and whether it is safe — and you need all four in the room before you scale it."

How it actually works

Building this view starts with a step most teams skip: defining the unit of the task precisely. For Vaani, the unit was one support ticket, and Tara's team had to decide, in writing, what counted as "resolved" — a reply that generated no reopened ticket within forty-eight hours. That window is a judgment call, and a different window would move the number, which is why it has to be written down before anyone looks at results.

Second, the team instruments the human–AI interaction itself, not just the outcome. Every draft was tagged into one of three buckets: sent unedited, edited then sent, or discarded and rewritten. For the edited bucket, Vaani's system also logged the kind of edit made — factual correction, tone, or added detail — because an edit rate without a reason attached tells you something changed but not whether the AI was wrong or merely generic.

Third comes cost, and the step most teams shortcut is including labour, not just the API bill. Vaani's inference cost per draft was thirty-five paise, trivially small; the real cost was the minute or two of an agent's time reading, judging and possibly rewriting the draft, priced at Vaani's fully loaded agent cost of about four hundred fifty rupees an hour. A cost-per-task number that ignores that minute is measuring the vendor's invoice, not the feature.

Fourth, safety is sampled, not assumed. Because no team can re-read every ticket, Vaani ran an automated policy checker across all drafts, flagging language that promised refunds outside policy, misstated the return window, or named a competitor, and had a human auditor review a statistically sized sample of flagged and unflagged tickets each week — the step usually left implicit is deciding, before launch, how large that sample must be to catch a rare but costly failure with confidence.

A worked example

In the pilot week Tara pulled for the board, Copilot produced drafts for 10,000 tickets. Of those, 41% (4,100) were sent unedited, 47% (4,700) were edited then sent, and 12% (1,200) were discarded and rewritten. Average handling time was 45 seconds for the unedited bucket, 110 seconds for the edited bucket, and 240 seconds for the discarded bucket — the last figure being identical to the pre-Copilot baseline, since a discarded draft means the agent wrote the reply the old way.

Add inference cost of thirty-five paise across 10,000 drafts — ₹3,500 — and total weekly cost comes to about ₹1.27 lakh, against a pre-Copilot baseline of 10,000 tickets at 240 seconds each, or ₹3.00 lakh. That is a 58% reduction in drafting cost, the number that reached the board slide. Reopen-based task success, weighted across the three buckets, came to 89.1%, against a pre-Copilot baseline of 88% — flat, reassuring, and the second number the board saw.

Now change one input: swap the success metric from "no reopened ticket" to average customer satisfaction score, on Vaani's usual five-point scale. Weighting the same three buckets by CSAT gives 0.41×3.6 + 0.47×4.3 + 0.12×4.0 = 3.98, against a pre-Copilot baseline CSAT of 4.10. The reopen-based story said "flat, maybe slightly up." The CSAT-based story says "down, by about three percent." Both are honest measurements of the same eight months of data; they disagree because they define success differently, and the unedited bucket — the fastest, cheapest bucket, the one growing fastest as agents lean on Copilot — is the one dragging CSAT down while barely denting the reopen rate. Cost per task and reopen success both said "scale it." CSAT said "look closer before you do."

The nuances

Acceptance is not quality

An agent who sends a draft unedited might be doing so because it is excellent, or because they are busy, trust the tool by default, and are not reading closely. Vaani's own data suggests some of the second: the unedited bucket has the lowest reopen success and the lowest CSAT of the three. A rising acceptance rate is only good news once you have checked it against an independent quality signal.

Edit rate needs a reason attached

A bare edit rate cannot distinguish "the draft was a strong starting point that needed one factual tweak" from "the draft was unusable and the agent rewrote half of it." Vaani's tagging of edit type — factual correction, tone, added detail — turns one ambiguous number into three diagnosable ones.

Cost per task must include the human

Teams that report only the model's API cost are reporting a number that can look extraordinary while the feature quietly makes support more expensive, because the reviewing agent's time dwarfs the inference bill by three orders of magnitude in Vaani's own numbers.

The denominator changes the answer

Cost per task computed over drafts shown looks different from cost per task computed over all tickets, including the minority where Copilot was not triggered at all. Reporting the narrower denominator flatters a partial rollout.

Sample size determines what safety metrics can see

A weekly manual review of fifty tickets, common in early pilots, cannot reliably detect a two percent problem rate; it will report "zero incidents found" many weeks in a row purely by chance, and that silence gets mistaken for safety.

These four metrics interact, and optimising one can quietly damage another

A model tuned to raise acceptance rate can learn to produce blander, more generically agreeable replies that agents wave through — the acceptance number improves while task success and CSAT drift down, exactly the pattern Vaani is watching.

A pilot vertical rarely generalises cleanly

Apparel returns are a narrow, well-templated ticket type. Cost and success gains measured there routinely shrink once Copilot meets messier verticals like appliance warranty disputes, where the correct answer depends on facts not in the ticket.

What none of the four can tell you

None of these numbers, however carefully built, measures rare catastrophic failure or long-run brand trust. A 0.6% weekly error rate looks small in a table and can still mean several hundred customers a month receiving an incorrect promise — a tail risk that averages hide by design.

Consumer, B2B and marketplace — and early stage versus scale

A consumer AI feature, like a shopping assistant inside a retail app, usually runs with no human in the loop, so task success has to be inferred from downstream behaviour — did the user complete a purchase, did they ask the same question again — and safety is judged against a broad content policy applied at huge, largely automated scale. Vaani's product is the opposite case: a B2B agent-assist tool sold under contract, where a human always reviews the AI's output before it reaches a customer, cost per task is a direct line item against the seat economics Vaani sells to its clients, and safety is compliance-driven, because an enterprise customer will ask for an audit trail, not a content-policy summary. A marketplace feature, such as a product-recommendation engine on a two-sided platform, complicates the tree further, because task success has to be measured on both the buyer's side and the seller's side, and a change that lifts one can quietly hurt the other. Stage matters as much as business model: in Vaani's first year, one PM could eyeball a few hundred flagged tickets a week and call it safety monitoring; at ninety client accounts and rising, that same habit under-samples badly, and the four metrics stop belonging to one person — task success sits with product analytics, safety with Rhea's trust-and-safety function, cost with finance, and the only way the four numbers stay coherent is a named owner and a fixed cadence that combines them before any scaling decision, rather than four teams each bringing their own slide to the board.

Common mistakes

Scaling on cost alone. The symptom is a leadership team excited by a falling cost-per-ticket chart, as Sundar was. The underlying error is conflating efficiency with effectiveness — a cheaper wrong answer is not progress. The cheapest diagnostic is pulling task success and CSAT split by acceptance bucket before agreeing to any expansion.

Undersized safety sampling. The symptom is a monthly report reading "zero safety incidents," repeated for months, that feels reassuring. The underlying error is treating a small sample's silence as proof of safety rather than as a sample too small to detect the true rate. The diagnostic is a simple statistical power calculation: at Vaani's real error rate, a sample of fifty tickets would miss the problem more often than it catches it.

An edit rate with no reason codes. The symptom is a metric that creeps upward for months, triggering alarm that "the model is getting worse," when the real cause is a shifting mix of harder ticket types. The diagnostic is segmenting edit rate by ticket category and cohort before drawing any trend conclusion.

No named owner for the combined view. The symptom is three functions arriving at a quarterly review with three different numbers for the same feature. The diagnostic is asking, plainly, who owns this metrics tree and what decision it feeds — if the answer is unclear, the dashboard is decoration.

What good looks like

Two weeks later, a similar decision at a competing helpdesk vendor went differently. Its PM had built the safety sample size into the pilot design from day one, powered to detect a one percent error rate with reasonable confidence, and had segmented CSAT and reopen rate by acceptance bucket from the first week of data rather than the eighth month. When their cost-per-ticket number fell, the safety and quality numbers were already sitting next to it on the same page, reviewed by the same weekly forum that included product, trust and safety, and finance. The rollout that followed was staged by ticket category, with a written threshold — below which expansion continued automatically, above which it paused for review — agreed before the numbers came in, not argued about after.

Closing

Tara recommended against the sixty-day full rollout. She proposed instead an expansion to 60% of volume, with a mandatory human-review flag on any draft mentioning a refund amount or return-window date, a safety sample large enough to detect a 0.5% error rate with real confidence, and a three-week checkpoint against two written thresholds: reopen success no more than one point below baseline, and safety slip-through under 0.3% of drafts. Sundar was not thrilled about the delay; Rhea called it the first rollout decision she had seen made on the right evidence. Tara's own reasoning was simple: the cost chart was real, but it was one of four numbers, and the other three had not yet finished telling their story. What she needs to learn next is how to design the evals that generate the task-success labels in the first place, since a metric is only as trustworthy as the judgment behind "resolved" or "safe." Two questions worth sitting with: when your fastest, cheapest bucket is also your lowest-quality bucket, is that a rollout to accelerate or a defect to fix before it grows? And what would have to be true for a metric with no visible incidents this month to still be hiding a problem large enough to matter?

Vipani Seller Cloud: Listing Studio Before the Festive Sale

A decision case on combining task success, acceptance and edit rates, cost per task and safety into one view before a rollout.

1. Friday evening, Hyderabad

At twenty past seven on Friday, 26 September 2025, Sneha Raghunathan stood at the whiteboard in Vipani Seller Cloud's office off the Financial District road in Hyderabad, with the ORR traffic crawling below and four numbers written in blue marker. She had until Monday morning to tell the executive team whether Listing Studio — the company's AI listing writer — would be switched on by default for all 42,000 sellers on the platform before the festive sale season began.

The timing was not negotiable. Flipkart's Big Billion Days and Amazon's Great Indian Festival would open in the first week of October, and Meesho's festive push with them. Sellers who intended to add catalogue for the season would do it in the next ten days or not at all. If Listing Studio was to matter in 2025, it had to be default-on by 1 October. If Sneha said no, the next natural window was the spring wedding season, six months away, by which time two competitors would have shipped something similar.

The four numbers on the board were the ones she had spent the week assembling, and they did not agree with each other. Acceptance of AI-written listings was 68 percent. The draft cost ₹1.90 per listing. The share of published AI listings that a compliance reviewer would have flagged was 2.4 percent. And conversion on AI-written listings, measured over the six weeks since the opt-in beta began, was 0.9 percentage points below conversion on seller-written listings for the same categories.

2. The company

Vipani Seller Cloud was founded in Hyderabad in 2019 by two former marketplace operations managers who had watched small sellers lose money to the tedium of catalogue work. Its software sat between the seller and the marketplaces: a seller uploaded photographs and a few facts about a product, and Vipani pushed a correctly formatted listing to Flipkart, Amazon India, Meesho and, since 2023, to buyer applications on the ONDC network, then synchronised inventory, orders and returns back.

By September 2025 Vipani served about 42,000 sellers, of whom 9,400 paid, on plans from ₹1,199 to ₹14,999 a month. Annual recurring revenue was ₹78 crore. The customer base skewed to small and mid-sized businesses in Tiruppur, Surat, Jaipur, Moradabad and Ludhiana — apparel, home furnishings, brassware, costume jewellery — and to a growing tail of direct-to-consumer brands that had begun on Shopify and wanted marketplace distribution without hiring a catalogue team. A handful of larger accounts, including an exporter in Dubai called Yusra Home Traders that sold Indian home textiles into the Gulf, paid enterprise rates.

Listing Studio had shipped in beta on 11 August 2025. It read the seller's photographs and a short form — category, material, size range, price — and produced a marketplace-ready title, five bullet points, a long description and a filled attribute sheet, in English, with Hindi and Tamil variants available. The seller could publish it as written, edit it, or throw it away.

3. The situation

The beta had gone well by every measure the team looked at daily. Of the 1,850 sellers who switched it on, most kept it on. Time to create a listing fell from a median of eleven minutes to four. Acceptance — the share of generated drafts the seller published, with or without edits — settled at 68 percent after the first fortnight, which Aditi Menon, the data scientist in Toronto who had built the evaluation set, considered strong for a first release.

On Friday 19 September, a growth analyst circulated a routine category report and someone noticed a line nobody had asked for. Among sellers in the beta, listings created through Listing Studio were converting at 1.8 percent against 2.7 percent for listings those same sellers had written by hand in the same categories over the same weeks. On a base of 214,000 AI-written listings that had gone live, the gap was not trivial.

Three explanations were live within a day, and the case for each was reasonable. Kartik Iyer, the VP Engineering in Bengaluru, thought it was selection: sellers used Listing Studio for the products they cared least about, the long tail they would otherwise never have listed, so of course those converted worse. Aditi thought it was attribute quality — the generated attribute sheets were sometimes plausible but wrong, and marketplace search depends on attributes, so the listings were simply being shown less often. Lena Brandt, the designer in Berlin, thought it was voice: the AI wrote clean, generic English, and small Indian sellers had been writing listings with specific, slightly ungrammatical detail that buyers evidently found more convincing.

Meanwhile Farah Sheikh, the customer-success lead in Singapore, had been logging a different category of complaint. Eleven sellers had been contacted by a marketplace quality team about listings with incorrect attributes, and two had had listings temporarily suppressed. In one instance an AI-generated description for a set of bedsheets had asserted a thread count that the seller had never supplied, and in another a stainless-steel serving bowl had been described as "food-grade certified" without any such certification existing. Neither had caused a customer complaint. Both, Farah pointed out, were exactly the kind of claim that attracts attention under the Legal Metrology packaged-commodities declarations and under advertising self-regulation, and Yusra Home Traders in Dubai had separately asked whether Vipani could certify that generated copy complied with UAE labelling requirements before it would enable the feature at all.

4. The people

Sneha Raghunathan, Head of Product, Hyderabad. Four years at Vipani, previously a category manager at a large retailer. She owns the recommendation and believes the company has been measuring the feature's convenience rather than its value.

Kartik Iyer, VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Responsible for the infrastructure bill, which at beta volumes is ₹4.1 lakh a month and at full default-on volumes would be roughly ₹31 lakh a month. He wants the rollout, partly because the fixed engineering cost is already spent, and he wants a cheaper model.

Aditi Menon, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto. Built the 400-listing evaluation set and reports 91 percent rubric quality. She is uneasy that the eval set was drawn from well-photographed apparel and home listings and contains almost none of the brassware and hardware categories where sellers have complained most.

Farah Sheikh, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Sees every seller escalation. She wants a human confirmation step on regulated attributes and is willing to accept a slower rollout to get it.

Vikram Chadha, Head of Sales, New Jersey, selling to Indian exporters and diaspora-facing brands in North America. He has three enterprise deals in the pipeline where an AI listing capability is named in the requirements, and he has already demonstrated it.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — The listing funnel, beta cohort, 11 August to 21 September 2025

Source: Vipani product analytics. "Eligible" means a listing the seller began in Listing Studio. Listings that were published but later suppressed by a marketplace quality process are counted as published but not as live. The 59,400 published listings that did not become live were mostly duplicates and image-quality rejections.

Exhibit 1 is where the argument about denominators begins. Read acceptance as published over drafts generated, and it is 71.6 percent. Read it over listings started, and it is 68.0 percent. Read the number that Sneha thinks matters — live and searchable after seven days — and the feature is carrying only 53 percent of the work a seller asked it to do. The gap between 68 and 53 is 59,400 listings that a seller believed were done and were not.

Exhibit 2 — Cost per listing and cost per outcome, September 2025 run rate

Projection assumes 68 percent of sellers use the feature on 70 percent of new listings during the festive period.

Exhibit 2 restates the same spending three ways and makes Kartik's and Sneha's positions visible as arithmetic rather than temperament. At ₹1.90 a draft, against an average plan price of ₹2,100 a month, the feature looks cheap. At ₹3.40 per listing that actually goes live and can be found by a buyer, and ₹31 lakh a month across the platform — about ₹3.7 crore a year against ₹78 crore of revenue — it is a material line that must be justified by something.

Exhibit 3 is the number Sneha finds hardest to hold beside the other two. A 2.4 percent serious-finding rate sounds small until it is multiplied by festive volume: on the projected 1.1 million AI listings in October, it is roughly 26,000 listings carrying a claim somebody would have to correct. And the concentration matters more than the level. Sixty-six percent of the serious findings sat in the categories Aditi's evaluation set barely covered.

6. The options

Option A — Default-on for all sellers from 1 October. Vipani captures the festive catalogue rush, Vikram closes his three enterprise deals, and the feature reaches the scale at which the conversion question can be answered properly. The costs are equally clear: ₹31 lakh a month of inference against a conversion effect that is currently negative and unexplained, and roughly 26,000 listings a month that a compliance reviewer would flag, in the season when marketplaces watch quality most closely.

Option B — Default-on in selected categories, with guardrails. Turn the feature on by default only for apparel and home furnishings, where the evaluation set is representative and serious findings run at 0.9 percent; keep it opt-in elsewhere; require the seller to confirm generated attributes before publish; keep a 10 percent holdout of sellers who do not get the default. Vipani reaches perhaps 60 percent of the festive volume, holds the compliance exposure down, and — because of the holdout — will actually know in November whether the conversion gap was selection or quality. The cost is a less impressive announcement and a visibly partial answer for Vikram's prospects.

Option C — Hold the rollout, fix attribute grounding, ship in November. Spend six weeks constraining generated attributes to values the seller has supplied or that can be read from the marketplace's own taxonomy, extend the evaluation set to the weak categories, and build the compliance checker Farah wants. Vipani misses the festive season entirely and ships into a quiet market, but ships something it can defend. Kartik's team loses six weeks of other roadmap, and two competitors ship first.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Vipani has been reporting acceptance at 68 percent. What would you report instead, and on what denominator, to describe honestly what Listing Studio is doing for a seller?

2. Three explanations were offered for the conversion gap — selection, attribute quality and voice. What single piece of evidence would most efficiently discriminate between them, and can Vipani obtain it before Monday?

3. Exhibit 2 shows the same spending at ₹1.90, ₹2.66 and ₹3.40. Which figure belongs in the board pack, and what does the choice imply about who owns the gap between them?

4. Which option would you recommend to Sneha, and what would you commit to measure weekly through October so that the recommendation could be reversed on evidence rather than on argument?

8. A note for the learner

This case is a test of whether a product manager can hold four families of measurement in one view: did the user's task actually get done (task success), did the user take what the machine produced and how much did they change it (acceptance and edit), what did it cost per unit of real output (cost per task), and how often was the output wrong in a way that matters (safety). Vipani has a number in each family. Its error is that the numbers live on different dashboards, with different owners, computed on different denominators, so no one has been able to see the trade.

A well-reasoned answer starts by fixing the unit of work. A listing drafted is not the unit; a listing live, searchable and correctly attributed is. Once that is the denominator, three of Sneha's four numbers change meaning at once. Acceptance falls from 68 to 53 percent. Cost rises from ₹1.90 to ₹3.40. And the conversion gap becomes testable rather than rhetorical, because a listing that is live but wrongly attributed is precisely the mechanism Aditi proposed.

A defensible path is Option B, and the reasoning runs as follows. The conversion gap is currently unexplained, and an unexplained negative on the company's core value metric is not a reason to stop but is a reason not to scale. The compliance findings are concentrated — 11 percent of volume carrying 66 percent of serious findings — which means a category restriction removes most of the risk at a fraction of the cost of a full delay. And the holdout is the cheapest thing on the table: ten percent of sellers left on the old flow costs Vipani almost nothing in October and is the only instrument that will settle the selection-versus-quality argument in November, when the same decision will come up again for the spring season with far more revenue attached.

Sneha should go into Monday's meeting with one table, not four dashboards: acceptance over listings started, share live at seven days, cost per live listing, and sampled severity-4-and-5 rate by category — each with a named owner, a weekly cadence, and the decision it gates. That last column is what turns a set of numbers into a rollout plan. It is also what allows her to say yes to Vikram in October and still be able to say no in November, if the evidence turns.

Product Metrics for AI Features

An extended treatment · Vachan Credit Systems, Mumbai and Zarurat Bazaar, Bengaluru · 2026

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On 14 April 2026, Meghna Iyer, director of product at Vachan Credit Systems, sat with two pages of numbers that disagreed. Vachan sold loan-origination software to twenty-three non-banking financial companies across India, and its newest feature, Vachan Vivek, read a borrower's bank statements, GST returns and bureau report and drafted a credit summary with a recommendation; a credit officer then approved it, edited it, or wrote their own. Some 46,000 files a month passed through Vivek, and officer time per file had fallen from thirty-eight minutes to just over twenty-three — a number Aditya Ranade, the chief revenue officer, had already sold two renewals on. Farida Kapadia, who ran risk, held the other page: an audit of four hundred Vivek-drafted files found five with a material misstatement of borrower income or undisclosed liability — 1.25 per cent — against 0.6 per cent for human-only files. Both pages were true. The board wanted one recommendation by Friday.

Eleven days later and eight hundred kilometres south, Kabir Sheth, vice-president of product at Zarurat Bazaar, faced a decision that looked nothing like Meghna's and was the same one. Zarurat was a grocery app with 4.1 million monthly users, competing for the same Tier-1 basket as Blinkit and Instamart. Its assistant, Zarurat Sakhi, took a request in Hindi, Kannada or English — "biryani for six on Sunday, budget eight hundred" — and built a cart, with no human reviewing anything. Sessions using Sakhi converted 31 per cent of the time against 24 per cent for search-only sessions, a gap his analytics lead, Anusha Rao, had reported every Monday since January. Inference cost ₹2.40 a conversation across 1.9 lakh conversations a day. The CEO wanted Sakhi on the home screen; Anusha wanted to talk about a holdout.

Meghna's feature had a human in the loop, a regulator watching and a twelve-month lag between output and outcome. Kabir's had none of the three. Both teams were about to find that their headline number was not measuring what they thought, and that the fix was not a better number but a different structure of numbers.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

The claim at the centre of this topic is narrow. For a feature whose output is generated rather than retrieved, no single product metric is decision-grade, because the ways such a feature can fail are not correlated with each other. Ordinary software that is fast, used and completed is almost certainly working. A generative feature can be fast, used, completed, confidently wrong, quietly expensive and unsafe at once, and each state is invisible to the metric that catches the others. The practice that follows is to hold four quantities together — task success, acceptance and edit behaviour, fully loaded cost per resolved task, and a measured rate of harmful output — and to make no scaling decision from fewer than all four.

Each of the four arrived from a different discipline and carries its parent's assumptions. Task success descends from human-factors work and Google's HEART framework (2010), which insisted user experience needed several axes. Acceptance and edit rate came from machine translation and code completion, where post-editing distance was the working quality proxy for two decades before copilots made it a product metric. Cost per task is unit economics, urgent only since serving a user got more expensive the more they used the product. The safety rate is the oldest: acceptance sampling, the statistical quality control of Dodge, Romig and Deming, in which you never inspect every unit and must therefore reason explicitly about what a clean sample proves. Over all of it sits Goodhart's observation that a measure which becomes a target ceases to be a good measure.

The eval-first school holds that ground truth lives offline, in a curated labelled set, and product metrics are lagging confirmation. It will sign: "a regression on the eval set should block a release, whatever acceptance says." It will not sign: "a high eval score is evidence of value."

The behaviour-first school holds the reverse: what people do with the output is the only signal that survived contact with reality. It will sign: "if the officer sends the summary unedited and the loan performs, the feature worked." It will not sign: "a test set built by the model's own team can tell you whether to ship."

The unit-economics school treats cost per resolved task as the only metric with a defensible denominator. It will sign: "an AI feature that does not lower cost per resolved task or raise revenue per task is a research project." It will not sign: "quality improvements justify themselves."

The assurance school, where Farida Kapadia sits, argues the tail dominates the mean. It will sign: "a savings figure without an interval on the harm rate is not a business case." It will not sign: "zero incidents observed means safe."

The four are not positions on a spectrum. They disagree about what counts as evidence, which is why their arguments rarely resolve by collecting more of the same data.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Start with Vachan, where the human in the loop makes every step visible. The first move is to fix the unit and the outcome horizon in writing before looking at data: Vachan's unit was one credit file, and its outcome was that the officer's decision stands without committee rework and the loan, if disbursed, is not thirty days past due within ninety — a clause that makes task success lagging, so the team can never hold a current reading of it. The second move is reason codes: Vivek logged each draft as sent unedited, lightly edited or heavily reworked, and recorded which field an edit changed. The third is the cost calculation, where most teams stop too early.

The fourth move converts the safety rate into the same currency. The audit found 1.25 per cent against a human baseline of 0.6, an increment of 0.65 points. Farida's team estimated that a material misstatement produces a wrongly approved loan one time in six; at a ₹6.2 lakh ticket and 55 per cent loss given default that loan costs ₹3.41 lakh, so a misstatement carries an expected cost near ₹56,800. The increment is therefore 0.0065 × 56,800 = ₹369 per file of added expected credit loss, against ₹184 of saving.

The interval is the heart of the matter and the step most teams leave implicit. Five findings in four hundred files gives a Wilson 95 per cent interval on the true rate of 0.54 to 2.89 per cent. At the lower bound Vivek is safer than the baseline and nets ₹221 a file; at the upper bound it destroys ₹1,117 a file, or ₹5.1 crore a month. The remedy is arithmetic: halving a binomial interval takes four times the sample, and auditing 1,500 files at ₹900 each costs ₹13.5 lakh against a decision worth ₹85 lakh a month in savings and up to ₹5 crore a month in risk.

The same logic gives the sampling rule. With zero failures in n samples, the 95 per cent upper bound on the true rate is about 3/n — the rule of three. Fifty clean reviews a week show only that the rate is below six per cent; a claim below 0.3 per cent takes a thousand.

The consumer case differs in one decisive respect: with no reviewer, acceptance must be inferred from behaviour, and behaviour is selected. Anusha Rao's seven-point gap compared users who chose to open Sakhi with users who did not. In May she hid the assistant entry point from a random 5 per cent of eligible users. The true lift was 1.8 points, not 7.0; the remaining 5.2 were selection, because people who reach for an assistant when planning a Sunday meal were already going to buy.

At an order value of ₹640 and 18 per cent contribution margin, an order contributes ₹115; a 1.8-point lift on 1.9 lakh sessions is 3,420 extra orders, or ₹3.94 lakh a day, against an inference bill of ₹4.56 lakh. Sakhi was losing ₹62,000 a day, ₹2.3 crore a year, while the naive figure made it look like ₹10.8 lakh a day of profit. Same feature, same month: the whole difference was the counterfactual.

4. When the four-metric view applies, and when it misleads

The approach rests on four conditions, each testable, and worth applying to both companies rather than asserting.

One: the task has a unit and a checkable outcome. Vachan passes cleanly — one file, one decision, one repayment record. Zarurat passes awkwardly: a conversation is a unit, but "did the user get what they needed" is observable only through purchase, and a user who abandons because Sakhi misread a constraint leaves the same trace as one whose phone rang.

Two: the counterfactual is observable. Zarurat passes, because a holdout is cheap and ethical. Vachan fails partially, and this is the deepest flaw in its measurement: the lender never learns how a rejected applicant would have repaid, so task success is estimable only on the approved population. A model that becomes subtly more conservative improves measured performance while shrinking the book, and no instrumentation on approved files will reveal it.

Three: harm is detectable within the decision cadence. Vachan fails again — credit harm surfaces over twelve to twenty-four months while rollout decisions are quarterly, which is why the audited misstatement rate exists as a leading proxy. Zarurat fails differently: a substitution or allergen error is detectable only if the customer complains, and most do not.

Four: volume supports estimation at the decision cadence. Zarurat passes for conversion and fails for rare harms; Vachan fails for both until it enlarges the audit.

The view becomes actively misleading in three situations: when the feature changes who uses the product, so a metric improves because a harder segment stopped showing up; when the lag between output and outcome exceeds the decision cadence, so the team optimises the proxy it can see — usually acceptance, the proxy most easily gamed by a model that learns to be agreeable; and on exploratory launches, where the purpose is learning and a cost-per-task gate kills options whose value was never going to appear in that quarter's ledger.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

The clean picture assumes one product, one team and one ledger. Real companies violate all three.

Multi-product and shared models. When a platform team owns the model and three product teams build on it, a guardrail change for one feature moves the metrics of the others and no dashboard records why. Vachan hit this in February: the platform team tightened a refusal policy for a compliance product, Vivek's heavy-rework rate jumped four points overnight, and the product team spent nine days investigating its own prompt. The fix is a change log keyed to the metrics' own timestamps; most organisations claim one, few have one a PM can read.

Two-sided markets. Talaash Marketplace, in home services, shipped a feature that rewrote provider profiles into polished copy. Provider metrics improved unambiguously: rewritten listings drew 34 per cent more enquiries. Buyer metrics moved the other way — when every plumber's profile reads like the same confident paragraph, the copy stops carrying information, and buyers took longer to choose and cancelled more after booking. The unit of success is the matched transaction both sides are glad about, which is never what either dashboard shows.

Regulated contexts. Under the RBI's digital lending framework a lender must explain an adverse decision and evidence the data behind it, which turns a metrics problem into an evidence problem: Vachan had to produce, per file, the source page for every number in the summary. That compliance requirement became the team's most effective quality intervention, because officers could verify a figure in seconds instead of re-reading a bank statement.

Hardware plus software. Yantrika Devices put a driver-assistance model on a dashcam sold to fleet operators. Inference runs on the device, so cost per task is capital amortised over the unit's life, and the metric that matters is cost per false alert: a driver warned wrongly four times a shift stops listening by the fifth. Telemetry is sampled because rural bandwidth is scarce, so the safety denominator is an estimate of an estimate.

AI-native products. When the model is the product there is no non-AI baseline, so cost per task becomes gross margin and task success becomes the north star rather than one of four. The quartet still applies, with the comparison removed — which makes absolute thresholds and longitudinal trends carry the weight a control group would otherwise bear.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Acceptance measures the reviewer's workload as much as the model's quality. The tell-tale is temporal: acceptance at Vachan rose four points in the last week of every quarter and fell back in the first week of the next. Volume pressure, not model improvement. The obvious reading is wrong because acceptance is a decision made by a busy human under a time constraint, and anything that changes the constraint moves the metric without touching the output.

Edit distance is not edit importance. A rewritten paragraph of tone is cosmetic; changing "₹4.2 lakh" to "₹2.7 lakh" is the whole file. The tell-tale is harm concentrated in the small-edit tail: at Vachan, files with one- or two-token edits carried higher downstream delinquency than files rewritten wholesale, because a heavy rewrite meant the officer had done the work properly.

Cost per task must be cost per resolved task. The tell-tale is two curves diverging: cost per conversation falling while cost per resolved issue rises, which happens whenever a cheaper model produces more retries. Sakhi's first cost cut lowered per-turn cost 40 per cent and raised average turns from 8 to 13; the denominator absorbed the gain.

The baseline drifts, so the counterfactual must be permanent. Teams run a holdout for two weeks at launch and retire it. The tell-tale is an "AI improvement" in a quarter when the control group, had it existed, would also have improved — staff get better, mix softens, seasonality helps. Zarurat now keeps a permanent 3 per cent holdout as the fixed cost of knowing anything.

Safety rates have a denominator problem that changes the decision. A rate of 0.2 per cent per response sounds negligible; per user per month, for someone with seventy interactions, it is 13 per cent — one user in eight meeting a bad output monthly. The tell-tale is a team that reports only the per-output figure. Both are correct; only one predicts complaints.

Offline eval scores and product metrics decouple, usually after the second or third model change. The tell-tale is a widening gap: eval score climbing while acceptance flattens. The cause is rarely mysterious — the team has been iterating against the eval set, so it has become a training signal rather than a test. An expert reads persistent decoupling as evidence the eval set has expired, not that acceptance is noisy.

An LLM judge inherits the blind spots of the model it judges. Raw agreement flatters: a judge agreeing with human labels 88 per cent of the time, when 90 per cent of outputs are fine, may have a Cohen's kappa near 0.3 — barely better than always guessing the majority class. The tell-tale is a judge from the generator's own model family, scored only on aggregate agreement. Report agreement separately on the minority class, where every decision that matters lives.

Most metric movements are mix shifts. When every segment improves and the aggregate falls, the composition changed. Vivek's overall acceptance fell 2.6 points in March while acceptance rose within all four lender segments, because one large client with unusually clean documents cut volume. The tell-tale is a trend that reverses under segmentation; the obvious reading would have rolled back a model that was fine.

Reviewers habituate, so human-in-the-loop quality decays on a schedule. Acceptance rises with an officer's tenure on the tool while audited quality stays flat or falls — the vigilance decrement familiar from aviation and radiology. The tell-tale is a cohort chart by weeks since onboarding. It is why the audit sample must be drawn from accepted outputs too, not only flagged ones: the accepted pile is where habituation hides.

7. How this differs across product types and stages

In consumer products the reviewer is absent, so acceptance must be reconstructed from behaviour and the dominant risk is selection; the right investment is a permanent holdout rather than a bigger dashboard. In B2B products a reviewer exists and the acceptance signal is rich, but contaminated by that reviewer's incentives, and the dominant risk is habituation. In enterprise and regulated settings the safety metric must be auditable rather than merely estimated: procurement will ask for the sampling protocol, and "we review some outputs weekly" fails the question. On platforms ownership fragments and attribution across teams binds. In marketplaces the unit of success spans two parties. In hardware inference is capital and telemetry is sampled. In AI-native products the quartet collapses toward two — task success and gross margin — with safety as a licence to operate.

Where the difference is not real it should be said plainly: the statistics do not change. The rule of three, the Wilson interval and the counterfactual requirement are identical for a dashcam and a grocery assistant; what changes is what a sample costs and how long an outcome takes to arrive. By stage, the honest difference is who can hold four numbers in one head. At Vachan's seed stage one PM read every flagged file; at twenty-three clients that habit under-sampled by an order of magnitude, and the metrics dispersed to analytics, risk, finance and platform. What keeps them coherent is unglamorous: one named owner for the combined view, a fortnightly forum, and a written rule about what each number must show before the rollout advances.

8. Three worked examples

Rakshan Insure Cloud: the fifth term. Rakshan built a triage model routing 40,000 motor claims a month, averaging ₹28,000, to fast-track settlement or investigation. Fast-tracking saves ₹310 of handling and four days of cycle time per claim, and lets some fraudulent claims through. The team tuned the threshold and built the ledger below.

The ledger says 0.90. The product manager argued for 0.80, because the table prices only two of the four metrics and omits the customer: at 0.80, eighteen points more claimants — 7,200 households a month — settle four days sooner, and renewal rates are sensitive to settlement speed. The ₹13 lakh a month difference is the price of that experience, and the useful move was to state it as a price rather than argue about whether the model was good.

Sopaan Learning: optimising the wrong one. Sopaan sold an essay-feedback tool to 340 CBSE-affiliated schools and made teacher acceptance its headline metric, driving it from 58 to 91 per cent across three model versions. The mechanism was visible only in hindsight: feedback became warmer, more general and harder to disagree with, so teachers approved it without reading closely. The metric nobody owned — whether a student made a substantive revision within seven days — fell from 27 to 19 per cent. Parents noticed before the product team did, and two school-board renewals worth ₹1.1 crore of annual revenue were lost. Recovery took two quarters: acceptance became a diagnostic, revision rate the headline, and a monthly blind audit was added in which two teachers scored 120 anonymised samples against a rubric, reporting inter-rater kappa so the audit's own reliability was visible. Acceptance fell to 63 per cent; revision rate rose to 44. Acceptance measures friction, and friction is sometimes the product.

Zarurat's recovery. Faced with a feature losing ₹62,000 a day, Kabir did not kill it. Anusha's turn-level analysis showed 72 per cent of conversations were simple retrieval — one item, a substitution, a reorder — and only 28 per cent needed real composition. Routing the simple majority to a distilled model at ₹0.55 cut blended cost from ₹2.40 to ₹1.07 a conversation, or ₹2.03 lakh a day. The re-run holdout measured a lift of 1.6 points, indistinguishable from 1.8, so contribution held near ₹3.50 lakh a day. A ₹2.3 crore annual loss became a ₹5.4 crore gain with no change to the model that had absorbed eight months of attention.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Scaling on the cost curve alone. Early sign: the only AI chart in the leadership deck trends down and to the right. Diagnostic: what is the fully loaded cost per resolved task, and what happened to quality within each acceptance bucket? Late cost, at Vachan's volumes: ₹1.7 crore a month of unrecognised expected credit loss.

Reporting a comparison no experiment supports. Early sign: a metric phrased as "users who used X versus users who did not." Diagnostic: where is the randomisation? Late cost: Zarurat spent eight months and ₹11 crore of inference on a business case negative from week one.

Mistaking a clean sample for a safe system. Early sign: "zero incidents" repeated at an unchanged sample size. Diagnostic: what upper bound does this sample support, and what would that rate cost us? Late cost: the incident is found by a regulator or a journalist instead of the team.

Optimising the most legible metric. Early sign: one number improving faster than everything else while the others go quiet. Diagnostic: which metric would deteriorate if this one were gamed, and is anyone watching it? Late cost: Sopaan's ₹1.1 crore.

Letting the metrics tree lose its owner. Early sign: three functions arriving at a review with three numbers for one feature. Diagnostic: who owns this view, at what cadence, for which decision? Late cost: decisions default to whoever's number is loudest, usually cost.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether acceptance rate deserves to be a headline metric. For: it is the only signal available at the moment of use, cheap, high-volume, and in code completion it correlates respectably with self-reported productivity. Against: it measures the reviewer's state, is gameable by blandness, and rises as vigilance falls. For the sceptics to be wrong, acceptance would have to stay correlated with independently audited quality across time and reviewer tenure. At Sopaan the correlation went negative; at Vachan it held two quarters and then decayed.

Whether offline evals or online metrics hold veto power. The eval-first camp notes that online metrics move for a dozen reasons unrelated to the model, so releasing on them means releasing on noise; the behaviour-first camp notes that eval sets decay and that none has ever predicted a novel failure mode. Both are right about the other's weakness. The unresolved question is empirical: how fast does a team's eval set lose predictive power? Those who measure it, by correlating eval deltas with subsequent acceptance deltas as in Fig. 4, find the half-life varies enormously by domain.

Whether expected cost of harm belongs in the same ledger as savings. Farida Kapadia's position is that pricing harm in rupees is the only way to make it compete with a savings number in a boardroom. The opposing view is that pricing harm licenses it: once a misstatement costs ₹56,800, savings can always be found that exceed it, and some harms — a discriminatory pattern in credit decisions, a health claim that injures someone — should be hard constraints rather than terms in a sum. For the pricing view to hold, the tail of the harm distribution must be bounded. For credit files it roughly is. For a consumer health assistant it is not.

Whether a single north star is possible for AI features. One camp argues four metrics is four decisions and therefore none, and that teams need a composite — contribution margin per successful task, say; the other argues any composite hides the trade-off leadership most needs to see. The difference shows when two metrics conflict: composite teams compute, quartet teams convene.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in five visible ways. They write the decision rule before the data arrives — threshold, action if it is missed, person who decides — because a rule written afterwards is a rationalisation. They report intervals rather than points, and can say roughly how large a sample their claim requires. They keep a counterfactual running permanently and treat its cost as the price of knowing anything. They separate mix from level reflexively, so their first question about a movement is "which segments, and did the composition change?" And asked for one number they do not refuse: they give it, with the two conditions under which it would be the wrong one to act on. The competent practitioner builds the dashboard; the expert builds the argument the dashboard is meant to settle, then builds only the parts that settle it.

12. What they decided

Meghna Iyer recommended neither a pause nor full rollout. She proposed holding Vivek at its current footprint while commissioning a 1,500-file audit at ₹13.5 lakh, on the argument that the decision was worth ₹85 lakh a month and the present interval could not distinguish a gain from a disaster. Alongside it she made two product changes justified independently of the audit: every figure in a Vivek summary had to carry a citation to its source page, and officers had to attest explicitly to income and liability fields before a summary advanced. The first, borrowed from the compliance requirement, cut heavy rework; the second deliberately reduced acceptance, on the reasoning that acceptance had been measuring the wrong thing. Aditya Ranade kept selling the time saving, now with a footnote.

Kabir Sheth kept Sakhi, shipped the router, and made two structural changes: the Monday metric became contribution margin per assisted session, and a 3 per cent holdout became permanent, written into the experimentation platform so no future PM could switch it off. Anusha Rao's summary at the quarterly review was the sentence the topic turns on — the feature had been fine all along; the measurement had not.

Discussion questions

  • Meghna's audit will take six weeks and cost ₹13.5 lakh. If the board refuses it, what is the next-best evidence available to her, and what decision would it support?
  • Vachan cannot observe outcomes for rejected applicants. Does that make its task-success metric unusable, or usable with a stated caveat — and how would you bound the error?
  • Rakshan's product manager priced four days of settlement speed at ₹13 lakh a month. Should an experience effect nobody can measure in rupees ever outrank a ledger that can be?

13. Going deeper

  • What evals are and why PMs own them — every task-success and safety number here rests on a labelled judgement of "correct"; an unowned eval set is an unowned metric.
  • North Star metric — the discipline the quartet borrows and modifies; the original clarifies what is given up.
  • What makes a good metric — sensitivity, gameability and lag decided every argument above, and can be assessed before instrumentation.
  • Vanity vs actionable metrics — "conversations handled" and "acceptance rate" are the vanity metrics of the AI era; the test is whether a movement changes a decision.
  • GAME framework — the scaffolding for writing the decision rule before the data arrives.
  • Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — Zarurat's router changed unit cost, not quality; knowing which lever moved prevents crediting the model for it.
  • Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio — acceptance is a proxy with a shifting denominator, which is why it misled three companies here.
  • Attention, transaction, productivity games — Sakhi plays a transaction game, Vivek a productivity game, and the four metrics carry different weights in each.

Nadi Health Systems: The Note That Signs Itself

Pune, March 2026. An ambient clinical documentation product, four numbers that do not agree, a renewal in Dubai and a board meeting on Monday.

1. Sunday night, Aundh

On Sunday, 15 March 2026, at ten minutes to midnight, Ishaan Pradhan was sitting at his dining table in Aundh with three laptops open — his own, his wife's, and an old machine he kept because it still had a working copy of the 2021 pricing model. The board of Nadi Health Systems met at three o'clock on Monday afternoon at the company's office in Baner. Ishaan, Vice-President of Product, had forty minutes on the agenda and three things to say, and he had not yet worked out whether they were the same thing said three ways or three different things that happened to be arriving together.

The first was the rollout of Auto-Finalise, a capability that would let Nadi Scribe close a clinical note without a physician opening it, for note types classified as low-risk. Engineering had it ready. The design lead in Berlin had been pushing for it since October. It would, on Nadi's own numbers, cut a doctor's documentation burden by a further nine minutes a day.

The second was the renewal of Rawdha Health Group in Dubai, Nadi's largest single contract at ₹11.4 crore a year, which expired on 31 March. Farida Qureshi in Singapore had written on Friday evening that Rawdha's chief information officer wanted, before signing, "a documented measure of clinical accuracy that we can put in front of our own quality committee".

The third was a set of figures that Ishaan had asked for on Thursday and received on Saturday evening, which he had now read four times. Between December and February, cost per finalised note had fallen 34 percent, which was the single best number in the company. Over the same period, the sampled rate of clinically significant omissions in finalised notes had roughly doubled — from 1.1 percent to 2.3 percent — on a sample small enough that a statistician would call the movement suggestive rather than established. Priya Nair's evaluation suite, run weekly, had not moved at all. It sat at 94 percent, as it had since September.

Three numbers, three directions, one meeting. Ishaan made another cup of tea and opened the 2021 file.

2. How Nadi got here, and the decision that still binds it

Nadi Health Systems was founded in Pune in 2018 by Ishaan and a paediatrician, Dr. Meenakshi Sundaram, who had spent eleven years in outpatient medicine in Chennai and had formed the view that Indian doctors were spending a quarter of their clinical time producing documents nobody read. The first product was a dictation tool. By 2021 it had become Nadi Scribe: an ambient assistant that listened to a consultation with consent, produced a structured clinical note — history, examination, assessment, plan, prescription — and presented it to the physician for review and signature. A second module, Nadi Intake, collected symptom histories from patients in the waiting area.

The decision that still constrained everything was made in August 2021. Anandvan Hospitals, a nine-hospital chain across Pune, Nagpur and Indore, was ready to sign but would not accept per-seat licensing; its doctors' usage was too variable and its finance team had been burned by shelfware. Nadi's then-CEO agreed to price per finalised note: ₹18 for an outpatient consultation note, ₹34 for a discharge summary. It won the contract, and the model was so much easier to sell that Nadi extended it to every subsequent customer, including Ujjwal Clinics, a 240-clinic network in tier-two and tier-three towns, and Rawdha Health Group in Dubai.

Five years later the consequences were structural. Revenue scaled with note volume and so did inference cost, so gross margin was a per-note arithmetic that moved with model pricing. More awkwardly, a finalised note was simultaneously the revenue event, the product's success metric and the thing a physician's signature was supposed to certify. Nadi billed for finalisation, reported finalisation as success, and had no measure of whether a finalised note was a good note that was independent of the fact that somebody had pressed a button Nadi was paid for.

3. The industry around the product

Indian clinical documentation in 2026 sat inside four forces pulling in different directions. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission had made structured, interoperable records a policy objective, and hospitals that wanted to publish to the health-information exchange needed notes coded consistently. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had made consent for processing a consultation recording an explicit, auditable requirement, which Nadi handled with a spoken consent prompt at the start of every session and a per-hospital data-processing agreement. The National Medical Commission's telemedicine practice guidelines placed the responsibility for the clinical record squarely on the registered medical practitioner, which was the legal reason a signature existed at all. And the country's insurers, working under IRDAI, were tightening documentation requirements for cashless claims, so that a discharge summary with a missing comorbidity could delay a settlement by weeks.

The commercial market was crowded. The large hospital groups — Apollo, Fortis, Max Healthcare, Narayana Health — all had digital programmes and could build internally if they chose. Practo and Tata 1mg had consumer footholds and clinical relationships. Global scribe products had begun to sell into Indian private chains at prices that assumed American reimbursement rates and were finding the ₹18-per-note market bewildering. Indian IT services firms, Infosys and TCS among them, were integrating third-party scribes into hospital information systems as part of larger deals, which meant Nadi was sometimes a component and sometimes a competitor in the same account.

Nadi's exposure outside India was concentrated and growing. Rawdha Health Group's three hospitals in Dubai and Sharjah generated 18 percent of revenue at roughly 2.6 times the Indian per-note price. Greg Donnelly in New Jersey had two American pilots in discussion at prices that would be ten times the Indian rate, and had built his forecast on a gross margin figure supplied in January.

4. The situation, in order

The sequence matters, because at every point the team believed something that later turned out to be partly wrong.

September 2025. Priya Nair, the Toronto-based data scientist who owned evaluation, froze an evaluation set of 1,400 consultations — transcripts with gold-standard notes written by two physicians — and reported 94 percent on a composite rubric covering completeness, accuracy and coding. The set was assembled from Anandvan's Pune and Nagpur hospitals, where consultations were largely in English with Marathi interjections. At the time everyone believed the set was representative. It contained almost no Ujjwal Clinics material, where consultations ran in Hindi, Bhojpuri and heavy code-mixing, and it had not been refreshed since.

October 2025. Jonas Weber in Berlin proposed Auto-Finalise. His argument rested on a study his team ran with fourteen doctors: median time from note-ready to signature was four minutes eleven seconds, but the median time the note was actually on screen was nineteen seconds. Doctors were, in practice, signing without reading. Jonas's reading was that the review step was theatre and should be removed for low-risk notes. Dr. Meenakshi Sundaram's reading of the same finding was the opposite: that the review step was failing and should be repaired.

December 2025. The board set a gross-margin objective. Sarika Mehta, the CFO in Mumbai, told the executive team that cost per finalised note had to come down from ₹7.40 to under ₹5.00 by the end of the financial year, or the American pricing conversation would not survive diligence.

February 2026. Cost per finalised note came in at ₹4.88. Rohit Bhandari's platform team in Bengaluru had achieved it through three changes: aggressive prompt caching, a shorter note template for follow-up consultations, and the routing of what Rohit described in the sprint review as "a portion of low-complexity traffic" to a smaller distilled model. The portion was 22 percent. It was not mentioned in the monthly product review, because cost work was reported in the platform review, which product did not attend.

Late February 2026. Dr. Meenakshi's clinical governance function completed its quarterly sampled review. The rate of clinically significant omissions — a medication, an allergy, a comorbidity or a follow-up instruction present in the consultation and absent from the finalised note — had risen from 1.1 percent in December to 2.3 percent in February. The sample was 180 notes a month. Two of the three reviewers had changed in January, when the original reviewers returned to clinical duty.

6 March 2026. Anandvan's revenue-cycle team sent Farida a query: insurance claim queries on discharge summaries had risen from 6.1 percent to 8.4 percent of claims since January. They were not alleging causation. They were asking whether Nadi had changed anything.

13 March 2026. Rawdha's CIO asked for a documented accuracy measure before renewal.

5. The people

Ishaan Pradhan, VP Product, Pune. Position: the company cannot ship Auto-Finalise until it can measure note quality independently of finalisation. Incentive: his equity is meaningful and a failed renewal or a clinical incident would be attributed to him. Not saying: he has suspected since December that finalisation rate is a corrupted metric and did not raise it while it was the only number going up.

Dr. Meenakshi Sundaram, Co-founder and Chief Medical Officer, Chennai. Position: Auto-Finalise is unacceptable for any note type while the omission rate is moving, and the NMC guidelines make the physician's signature non-delegable in any case. Incentive: her professional reputation is on every note. Not saying: her own audit found that doctors at two Ujjwal sites were signing batches of forty notes in under three minutes, which means the safeguard she is defending is already not operating.

Rohit Bhandari, VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: the cost programme worked, the numbers are real, and the omission finding is within sampling noise on n=180. Incentive: his team's annual objective was the margin number and it has been met. Not saying: he knows the distilled-model routing coincided almost exactly with the omission increase, and he has asked an engineer, quietly, to pull the omission findings split by model.

8. The options as Ishaan sees them

By Sunday evening Ishaan had written three options on the back of the board agenda, and he was aware, in the way one is aware of a draught, that the list might be describing the wrong problem.

Option one: ship Auto-Finalise for follow-up notes only, from 1 April. It is the note type with the highest unedited rate, the lowest median edit distance and the lowest price sensitivity. It gives Jonas his result, gives Greg a differentiated capability for the American pilots, and gives Sarika another leg of margin because an unopened note consumes no physician time and can be generated on a cheaper template. It also means Nadi would be finalising — and billing for — notes that no human has seen, in the same quarter in which its only clinical instrument suggests omissions are rising, in the note type Exhibit 4 associates, weakly, with the distilled model.

Option two: hold Auto-Finalise, revert the distilled-model routing, and spend the next quarter building measurement. Refresh the evaluation set with Ujjwal audio and code-mixed dictation, raise the clinical sample from 180 to 1,000 notes a month with calibrated reviewers, instrument what a physician actually looks at rather than what they sign, and build a claim-outcome join with Anandvan. Cost per note returns to roughly ₹6.30, margin falls back toward 62 percent, the board deck is restated, and Greg's pricing conversation becomes harder. Rawdha gets a promise of a number rather than a number.

Option three: change the commercial model. Move from per-finalised-note to per-clinician-per-month, starting with the Rawdha renewal, so that Nadi's revenue stops being generated by the same event it uses to define success. This decouples the metric from the money and makes it possible, for the first time, to report a finalisation rate that nobody has an incentive to inflate. It also means renegotiating with a customer who is already looking at a competitor, in the fortnight before the contract lapses, and it puts ₹11.4 crore of the cleanest revenue in the company in play. Anandvan and Ujjwal would have to follow eventually, and Ujjwal's economics at 1.61 million notes a month across 240 low-margin clinics may not survive a per-clinician price at all.

What Ishaan had not written down, and kept returning to, was a fourth thing that was not an option so much as a doubt: that all three options assume the company knows what a good note is. Nadi measures whether a note was finalised, how much it was edited, what it cost and how often a reviewer finds an omission. None of those is the thing a patient or an insurer or a court would call quality, and the one instrument that comes closest — Dr. Meenakshi's sample — is 180 notes drawn from 3.5 million.
